    <div class="guide-header">
        <span class="ad-badge"><i class="fas fa-server"></i> Enterprise Security</span>
        <h1>Active Directory Security Hardening</h1>
        <p style="color: var(--text-muted); font-size: 1.1rem;">Defend the #1 enterprise attack target with tiered
            admin, Kerberos hardening, and attack detection strategies</p>
        <div style="margin-top: 1rem; color: var(--text-muted);">
            <span><i class="fas fa-book-open"></i> 28 min read</span> <span style="margin: 0 0.5rem;">|</span>
            <span><i class="fas fa-crosshairs"></i> Intermediate</span> <span style="margin: 0 0.5rem;">|</span>
            <span><i class="far fa-calendar-alt"></i> January 2026</span>
        </div>
    </div>

    <img src="/images/guides/active-directory-security-hardening.png" alt="Active Directory Security Hardening"
        class="featured-image"
        style="width: 100%; max-width: 100%; height: auto; border-radius: 12px; margin: 2rem 0; box-shadow: 0 10px 40px rgba(59, 130, 246, 0.2); border: 1px solid var(--border);" loading="lazy">

    <div class="warning-box">
        <strong><i class="fas fa-exclamation-triangle"></i> Critical Target:</strong> Active Directory is
        compromised in over 80% of enterprise breaches. If attackers own AD, they own everything. This guide
        provides practical hardening steps you can implement today.
    </div>

    <!-- Table of Contents -->
    <div class="toc">
        <h3><i class="fas fa-list-ul"></i> Table of Contents</h3>
        <ul>
            <li><a href="#why-ad">1. Why Active Directory is the Crown Jewel</a></li>
            <li><a href="#tiered-model">2. The Tiered Administrative Model</a></li>
            <li><a href="#privileged-accounts">3. Securing Privileged Accounts</a></li>
            <li><a href="#kerberos">4. Kerberos Hardening</a></li>
            <li><a href="#gpo-security">5. Group Policy Security</a></li>
            <li><a href="#common-attacks">6. Detecting Common AD Attacks</a></li>
            <li><a href="#monitoring">7. Monitoring and Alerting</a></li>
            <li><a href="#quick-wins">8. Quick Wins Checklist</a></li>
        </ul>
    </div>

    <h2 id="why-ad">1. Why Active Directory is the Crown Jewel</h2>

    <p>Active Directory (AD) is the identity and access management backbone for 95% of Fortune 500 companies. When
        attackers compromise AD, they gain:</p>

    <table>
        <thead>
            <tr>
                <th>What They Get</th>
                <th>Impact</th>
            </tr>
        </thead>
        <tbody>
            <tr>
                <td><strong>All user credentials</strong></td>
                <td class="severity-critical">Access to every account in the organization</td>
            </tr>
            <tr>
                <td><strong>Group memberships</strong></td>
                <td class="severity-critical">Ability to add themselves to any group</td>
            </tr>
            <tr>
                <td><strong>Computer accounts</strong></td>
                <td class="severity-high">Lateral movement to any joined system</td>
            </tr>
            <tr>
                <td><strong>GPO control</strong></td>
                <td class="severity-critical">Push malware to every endpoint</td>
            </tr>
            <tr>
                <td><strong>Certificate authority access</strong></td>
                <td class="severity-critical">Issue certificates for any user</td>
            </tr>
        </tbody>
    </table>

    <div class="info-box">
        <strong><i class="fas fa-lightbulb"></i> Think of it like this:</strong> Active Directory is like the master
        key system for a building. If someone steals the master key, they can open every door. AD security is not
        just an IT issue - it is a business survival issue.
    </div>

    <h3>The AD Attack Kill Chain</h3>

    <p>Attackers follow a predictable path when targeting AD:</p>

    <ol>
        <li><strong>Initial Access</strong> - Phishing, vulnerability exploitation</li>
        <li><strong>Credential Theft</strong> - Mimikatz, LSASS dumping</li>
        <li><strong>Reconnaissance</strong> - BloodHound, AD enumeration</li>
        <li><strong>Privilege Escalation</strong> - Kerberoasting, delegation abuse</li>
        <li><strong>Lateral Movement</strong> - Pass-the-hash, pass-the-ticket</li>
        <li><strong>Domain Dominance</strong> - DCSync, Golden Ticket</li>
    </ol>

    <h2 id="tiered-model">2. The Tiered Administrative Model</h2>

    <p>The tiered model is the foundation of AD security. It creates security boundaries that prevent attackers from
        moving from low-value to high-value targets.</p>

    <div class="tier-box tier-0">
        <h4><i class="fas fa-crown" style="color: var(--accent-red);"></i> Tier 0 - Domain Controllers and Identity
        </h4>
        <p><strong>What belongs here:</strong></p>
        <ul>
            <li>Domain Controllers</li>
            <li>AD FS, Azure AD Connect servers</li>
            <li>PKI/Certificate Authority servers</li>
            <li>Privileged Access Workstations (PAWs)</li>
            <li>Domain Admin and Enterprise Admin accounts</li>
        </ul>
        <p><strong>Rule:</strong> Tier 0 admins NEVER log into Tier 1 or Tier 2 systems.</p>
    </div>

    <div class="tier-box tier-1">
        <h4><i class="fas fa-server" style="color: var(--accent-orange);"></i> Tier 1 - Enterprise Servers</h4>
        <p><strong>What belongs here:</strong></p>
        <ul>
            <li>Application servers</li>
            <li>Database servers</li>
            <li>File servers</li>
            <li>Email servers</li>
            <li>Server admin accounts</li>
        </ul>
        <p><strong>Rule:</strong> Tier 1 admins can manage servers but not workstations or DCs.</p>
    </div>

    <div class="tier-box tier-2">
        <h4><i class="fas fa-desktop" style="color: var(--accent-green);"></i> Tier 2 - Workstations and Users</h4>
        <p><strong>What belongs here:</strong></p>
        <ul>
            <li>User workstations</li>
            <li>Laptops</li>
            <li>Help desk support</li>
            <li>Workstation admin accounts</li>
        </ul>
        <p><strong>Rule:</strong> Tier 2 admins only manage end-user devices.</p>
    </div>

    <h3>Implementing Tier Separation</h3>

    <pre><code># Create tiered admin groups

New-ADGroup -Name “Tier0-Admins” -GroupScope Global -Path “OU=Tier0,OU=Admin,DC=corp,DC=local” New-ADGroup -Name “Tier1-Admins” -GroupScope Global -Path “OU=Tier1,OU=Admin,DC=corp,DC=local” New-ADGroup -Name “Tier2-Admins” -GroupScope Global -Path “OU=Tier2,OU=Admin,DC=corp,DC=local”

Use GPO to restrict logon

Deny “Log on locally” for Tier0 admins on Tier1/Tier2 systems

Deny “Log on through Remote Desktop Services” similarly

    <h2 id="privileged-accounts">3. Securing Privileged Accounts</h2>

    <h3>Password Best Practices</h3>

    <table>
        <thead>
            <tr>
                <th>Account Type</th>
                <th>Minimum Length</th>
                <th>Rotation</th>
                <th>Storage</th>
            </tr>
        </thead>
        <tbody>
            <tr>
                <td>Domain Admin</td>
                <td class="severity-critical">25+ characters</td>
                <td>90 days</td>
                <td>Emergency break-glass only</td>
            </tr>
            <tr>
                <td>Service Accounts</td>
                <td class="severity-critical">25+ characters</td>
                <td>Use gMSA (automatic)</td>
                <td>Group Managed Service Accounts</td>
            </tr>
            <tr>
                <td>Tier 0 Admin</td>
                <td class="severity-high">20+ characters</td>
                <td>90 days</td>
                <td>PAM solution</td>
            </tr>
            <tr>
                <td>Tier 1/2 Admin</td>
                <td class="severity-medium">15+ characters</td>
                <td>90 days</td>
                <td>Password manager</td>
            </tr>
        </tbody>
    </table>

    <h3>Protected Users Group</h3>

    <p>Add all privileged accounts to the Protected Users security group:</p>

    <pre><code># Add admin to Protected Users

Add-ADGroupMember -Identity “Protected Users” -Members “AdminAccount”

Verify membership

Get-ADGroupMember -Identity “Protected Users”

    <p>Protected Users provides:</p>
    <ul>
        <li><i class="fas fa-check-circle" style="color: var(--accent-green);"></i> No NTLM authentication (prevents
            pass-the-hash)</li>
        <li><i class="fas fa-check-circle" style="color: var(--accent-green);"></i> No credential caching</li>
        <li><i class="fas fa-check-circle" style="color: var(--accent-green);"></i> No DES or RC4 encryption in
            Kerberos</li>
        <li><i class="fas fa-check-circle" style="color: var(--accent-green);"></i> Cannot be delegated</li>
    </ul>

    <div class="warning-box">
        <strong><i class="fas fa-exclamation-triangle"></i> Caution:</strong> Test Protected Users in a lab first.
        Some legacy applications may break when NTLM is disabled. Service accounts should use gMSAs instead of
        Protected Users.
    </div>

    <h3>LAPS for Local Admin Passwords</h3>

    <p>Local Administrator Password Solution (LAPS) ensures unique passwords on every machine:</p>

    <pre><code># Deploy LAPS via GPO

1. Install LAPS management tools

Install-WindowsFeature RSAT-AD-Tools

2. Extend AD schema (one-time)

Update-AdmPwdADSchema

3. Set permissions

Set-AdmPwdComputerSelfPermission -OrgUnit “OU=Workstations,DC=corp,DC=local”

4. Allow IT to read passwords

Set-AdmPwdReadPasswordPermission -OrgUnit “OU=Workstations,DC=corp,DC=local” -AllowedPrincipals “Tier2-Admins”

    <h2 id="kerberos">4. Kerberos Hardening</h2>

    <p>Kerberos is the authentication protocol for AD. Hardening it prevents many common attacks.</p>

    <h3>Kerberoasting Defense</h3>

    <div class="attack-box">
        <strong>Kerberoasting</strong> extracts service account password hashes from TGS tickets. Attackers request
        tickets for SPNs, then crack them offline.
    </div>

    <div class="defense-box">
        <ul>
            <li><strong>Use gMSAs</strong> - Automatic 240-character passwords that rotate automatically</li>
            <li><strong>Long passwords</strong> - 25+ characters for all service accounts</li>
            <li><strong>Monitor TGS requests</strong> - Alert on bulk ticket requests</li>
            <li><strong>Limit SPN accounts</strong> - Audit and remove unnecessary SPNs</li>
        </ul>
    </div>

    <pre><code># Find accounts with SPNs (potential Kerberoasting targets)

Get-ADUser -Filter {ServicePrincipalName -ne “$null”} -Properties ServicePrincipalName | Select-Object Name, ServicePrincipalName

Create a gMSA

New-ADServiceAccount -Name “svc-webapp” -DNSHostName "svc-webapp.corp.local" -PrincipalsAllowedToRetrieveManagedPassword “WebServers”

    <h3>AS-REP Roasting Defense</h3>

    <div class="attack-box">
        <strong>AS-REP Roasting</strong> targets accounts with Kerberos pre-authentication disabled, allowing
        attackers to request encrypted data crackable offline.
    </div>

    <div class="defense-box">
        <p>Ensure NO accounts have "Do not require Kerberos preauthentication" enabled:</p>
    </div>

    <pre><code># Find vulnerable accounts

Get-ADUser -Filter {DoesNotRequirePreAuth -eq $True} -Properties DoesNotRequirePreAuth

Fix vulnerable accounts

Set-ADAccountControl -Identity “VulnerableUser” -DoesNotRequirePreAuth $false

    <h3>Disable Weak Encryption</h3>

    <pre><code># Via GPO: Computer Configuration > Policies > Windows Settings >

Security Settings > Local Policies > Security Options

“Network security: Configure encryption types allowed for Kerberos”

Enable ONLY: AES128_HMAC_SHA1, AES256_HMAC_SHA1

Disable: DES_CBC_CRC, DES_CBC_MD5, RC4_HMAC_MD5

    <h2 id="gpo-security">5. Group Policy Security</h2>

    <h3>Critical GPO Hardening</h3>

    <table>
        <thead>
            <tr>
                <th>Setting</th>
                <th>Location</th>
                <th>Value</th>
            </tr>
        </thead>
        <tbody>
            <tr>
                <td>Disable LM hash storage</td>
                <td>Security Options</td>
                <td>Enabled</td>
            </tr>
            <tr>
                <td>LAN Manager auth level</td>
                <td>Security Options</td>
                <td>Send NTLMv2 only/Refuse LM and NTLM</td>
            </tr>
            <tr>
                <td>Credential Guard</td>
                <td>Device Guard</td>
                <td>Enabled with UEFI lock</td>
            </tr>
            <tr>
                <td>Remote Credential Guard</td>
                <td>Credentials Delegation</td>
                <td>Enabled</td>
            </tr>
            <tr>
                <td>Restrict NTLM</td>
                <td>NTLM Settings</td>
                <td>Audit then Deny</td>
            </tr>
        </tbody>
    </table>

    <h2 id="common-attacks">6. Detecting Common AD Attacks</h2>

    <h3>DCSync Attack</h3>

    <div class="attack-box">
        <strong>DCSync</strong> abuses domain replication permissions to request password hashes directly from a DC.
        Attackers use Mimikatz to impersonate a domain controller.
    </div>

    <div class="defense-box">
        <p><strong>Detection:</strong> Monitor Event ID 4662 for these GUIDs:</p>
        <ul>
            <li><code>1131f6aa-9c07-11d1-f79f-00c04fc2dcd2</code> - DS-Replication-Get-Changes</li>
            <li><code>1131f6ad-9c07-11d1-f79f-00c04fc2dcd2</code> - DS-Replication-Get-Changes-All</li>
        </ul>
        <p><strong>Prevention:</strong> Audit and restrict replication rights to only Domain Controllers.</p>
    </div>

    <h3>Golden Ticket Attack</h3>

    <div class="attack-box">
        <strong>Golden Ticket</strong> uses the KRBTGT hash to forge TGTs for any user, including non-existent ones,
        with any group membership.
    </div>

    <div class="defense-box">
        <ul>
            <li><strong>Rotate KRBTGT twice</strong> (with 10+ hour gap)</li>
            <li><strong>Monitor for TGT anomalies</strong> - Long lifetimes, impossible SIDs</li>
            <li><strong>Use Microsoft ATA/Defender for Identity</strong></li>
        </ul>
    </div>

    <pre><code># Reset KRBTGT password (do this twice, 10+ hours apart)

WARNING: May cause authentication issues - plan carefully

Reset-ADServiceAccountPassword -Identity krbtgt

Verify last password change

Get-ADUser krbtgt -Properties PasswordLastSet | Select-Object PasswordLastSet

    <h2 id="quick-wins">8. Quick Wins Checklist</h2>

    <p>Implement these changes today for immediate security improvement:</p>

    <div class="success-box">
        <h4><i class="fas fa-check-circle"></i> Week 1 Quick Wins</h4>
        <ul>
            <li>Add all Domain Admins to Protected Users group</li>
            <li>Find and fix accounts with "Do not require Kerberos preauthentication"</li>
            <li>Deploy LAPS to all workstations</li>
            <li>Disable LM hash storage</li>
            <li>Set LAN Manager to NTLMv2 only</li>
        </ul>
    </div>

    <div class="success-box">
        <h4><i class="fas fa-check-circle"></i> Month 1 Goals</h4>
        <ul>
            <li>Implement tiered admin model</li>
            <li>Convert service accounts to gMSAs</li>
            <li>Enable advanced audit policies</li>
            <li>Deploy Credential Guard on Windows 10/11</li>
            <li>Set up alerting for critical Event IDs</li>
        </ul>
    </div>

    <div class="success-box">
        <h4><i class="fas fa-check-circle"></i> Quarter 1 Goals</h4>
        <ul>
            <li>Deploy PAWs for Tier 0 administration</li>
            <li>Implement just-in-time (JIT) admin access</li>
            <li>Complete KRBTGT rotation</li>
            <li>Restrict NTLM across the environment</li>
            <li>Deploy Microsoft Defender for Identity or similar</li>
        </ul>
    </div>
